details.description: GHOST is a proof of concept, aiming to digitally control “smart fluidˮ to create instant reconfigurable molds from 3D mesh files for hobbyist manufacturing, capable of evolving into an industrial manufacturing process.

text: PROBLEM: The current standard for reconfigurable molds is the Pin Mold, where each pin requires an actuator, limiting it’s resolution. Liquid removes the resolution limitation, and electrorheological fluid (“smart fluid”) can be precisely controlled using voltage from electrodes.
IDEATION
PHASE 1 - Research, Testing, Iterating

SCIENCE - Electrorheological Fluids (ER) made up of cornstarch and vegetable oil, are extremely fine non-conductive but electrically active particles. When introduced to an electric field, ER’s viscosity changes in response. The GHOST basin has a 2D matrix of electrodes (pennies).

ELECTRONIC SCHEMATICS - In collaboration with Electrical Engineering Professor James Sherman @ AACC, I developed a voltage multiplier. ER requires high voltages which most DC power supplies do not provide. I was able to achieve 160 Volts through this multiplier and feed it to two electrodes.

CHALLENGES & REWORK - 160 Volts was not sufficient. There was little to no change in the viscosity of the ER fluid. After discussing the limitations, the results of my findings indicated most power supplies do not provide the necessary voltage, except for static electricity.
PHASE 2 - Rework, Software, Testing

STATIC ELECTRICITY - ER is often demonstrated with a charged balloon, which loses charge, and isn’t feasible for GHOST. Since ER only require high voltage (1-4kV/mm) and little to no current, researching how to use a Van de Graaff generator was the next step in this process.

SLICING SOFTWARE [https://github.com/Pink-Hat-Hacker/ghost-ui] - In anticipation for a fully functional prototype, and the future use of a microcontroller, I wrote a slicer in Python. It slices an STL along the x and y axis, mimicking the 2D basin, and plots the max z-axis points on a 3D graph. Using a surface plotter, the slicer hints the finished product.

TESTING & FUTURE ITERATIONS - To learn how a Van De Graaff generator worked, I created a version using household items. Phase 3 will involve an upgraded Van De Graaff generator to apply the current circuit schematic and test the basin 2D matrix.

details.description: DUO is a modular stationery system for makers & creatives. The structure is inspired by Japanese wood joinery which enables the connection of different tools depending on a users needs. It is an adaptable, versatile and evolving system.

text: PROBLEM - Creatives often purchase multiple tools by different brands to achieve their goals. An average consumer may not place much stake in what type of tool they are purchasing. If there was one system that provided quality, affordability and ease of use for various tools this would remove the need for multiple consumable products and increase sustainability.
experimenting with joinery in CAD (Fusion 360) & Sketches + Inspo

IDEATION - Focusing on longevity and an individual’s connection to their tools, DUO aims to provide customizable, space-saving, sustainable tools/devices that adapt to users needs. Aim for an intuitive connection mechanism that is satisfying, functional, and aesthetic.

CHALLENGES - Size and innovative mechanisms to ensure a reduced learning curve for users while maintaining a streamline profile. Manufacturing processes that are cost efficient, quality and work with the design. Designing functional mechanisms that can work with a range of materials. Multiple prototypes not fitting properly because of differing manufacturing processes or design.
Materials - PLA, RESIN, IRON infused PLA
Manufacturing - 3D Printing (Makerbot & Formlabs)
Designing - Fusion 360 & Blender
MINIMUM VIABLE PRODUCT
3 different tools: 2mm graphite pencil, ballpoint pen, utility device
produced using 3D printed PLA plastic with ferromagnetic properties
0.05mm offset for smooth joining
triangular body shape to prevent rolling & encourage proper holding position

details.description: allergen.ai aims to simplify allergen identification, using AI image recognition to identify food, ingredients, and cross reference them with an allergen database from a single photo upload. Designed with user convenience in mind, this experimental tool minimizes the reliance on possibly uninformed food providers.

text: The initial step was to research allergen information from a government directory. [https://www.fda.gov/food/nutrition-food-labeling-and-critical-foods/food-allergies]
Used the researched information to create a database using Firebase DB which helped to structure the next steps.
LogMeal [https://logmeal.com/api/] provided a well documented AI food recognition API and was tested using PostMan [https://www.postman.com/] and the Firebase database before coding.
Javascript, React, & Radix-UI came together to create a functioning, LIVE [http://pink-hat-hacker.github.io/allergen-ai/], website!

details.description: UDEL CS Capstone. Efficiently track microbots in 2 dimensions & implement z-axis tracking.

text: STAKEHOLDERS:
Dr. Sambeeta Das - Assistant Professor of Mechanical Engineering
Max Sokolich - PhD Candidate - Mechanical Engineering
[https://dasmicrobotlab.com/]
FIELD OF STUDY:
- Biomechanical Engineering
- Robotics & Controls
- Nanotechnology
- Micro robotic locomotion for applications In Vivo and In Vitro
OBJECTIVE:
- Efficiently track microbots in 2 dimensions & implement z-axis tracking.
CODING PROCESS: GUI
- Library, The GUI is made using Tkinter, a python library, that has tools to make an interface
- Functionality, Upload a prerecorded video, Instantaneously start the live video feed, Record and download a video, Alters the live camera parameters, Alters the control parameters of the feed

- Goal: Providing the client with control of different parameters and adding an option to change the contrast of the video to aid the tracker in “finding” the blurred microbot as they move on the z-axis.
CODING PROCESS: OpenCV PREPROCESSING:
To quantify distance in the z-axis, we chose to measure the “blur” of a microbot to represent its distance from the microscope lens.
We improved the existing contour-tracking preprocessing pipeline by adjusting it based on blur. This “dynamic” pipeline allowed us to accomplish two goals:
1) Measure the blur of a cropped microbot image to quantify distance
2) Modify the contour preprocessing based on a microbot’s blurriness to improve out-of-focus tracking
